nodes.label: The Vandal kingdom of Carthage
nodes.full: Gaiseric's kingdom: it crosses from Spain and takes Carthage in 439, seizing the West's richest grain province and its fleet; sacks Rome in 455; and destroys the huge East-West reconquest armada at Cape Bon in 468.
nodes.src: background — Prosper of Aquitaine; Procopius, 'De Bello Vandalico'

nodes.label: The Visigothic nation and kingdom of Toulouse
nodes.full: Alaric's people, pushed over the frontier by the Huns: they sack Rome in 410, are settled in Aquitaine as federates, fight beside Aetius against Attila, and by the 470s under Euric rule an independent kingdom that swallows most of Gaul and Spain.
nodes.src: background — see the visigoths-589-711 folio; Sidonius Apollinaris, 'Epistulae'

nodes.label: Attila's Hunnic empire
nodes.full: The steppe confederation that had driven the Goths west a generation earlier, now a tribute-extracting power on the Danube. Attila invades Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452, and on his death in 453 the empire disintegrates within a year.
nodes.src: background — Priscus fragments; Jordanes, 'Getica'

nodes.label: Honorius
nodes.full: Inherited throne age 10 on death of father Theodosius I; never led an army.
nodes.src: Coin evidence: solidus series minted Ravenna/Mediolanum. Court relocated to Ravenna 402.

nodes.label: Valentinian III
nodes.full: Crowned age 6; real power held first by his mother Galla Placidia, then by general Aetius.
nodes.src: Ivory diptych of consul Probus 406, later coins depict Valentinian. Murdered 16 Mar 455 — Hydatius Chronicle records date.

nodes.label: Avitus
nodes.full: Gallic aristocrat elevated by Visigoth king Theoderic II; deposed by general Ricimer.
nodes.src: Sidonius Apollinaris composed panegyric for him (Carmen VII, 456 AD). Deposed Oct 456.

nodes.label: Majorian
nodes.full: Last Western emperor to mount serious military campaigns; murdered by strongman Ricimer.
nodes.src: Seven novels (imperial laws) survive bearing his name and exact dates. Murdered 7 Aug 461.

nodes.label: Anthemius
nodes.full: Eastern candidate sent by Leo I to restore Western authority; killed in civil war with Ricimer.
nodes.src: Greek inscription from Rome survives. Sidonius Apollinaris: panegyric Carmen II delivered 1 Jan 468.

nodes.label: Julius Nepos
nodes.full: Last emperor recognised by both East and West; fled to Dalmatia when Orestes revolted.
nodes.src: Solidus coins. Assassinated in Dalmatia 480 per Cassiodorus.

nodes.label: Romulus Augustulus
nodes.full: Boy emperor installed by his father Orestes; deposed 4 Sep 476 by Odoacer.
nodes.src: Ennodius and Cassiodorus both record 4 Sep 476. Castellum Lucullanum = Pizzofalcone, Naples bay.

nodes.label: Arcadius
nodes.full: Inherited Eastern throne age 17; dominated by court factions.
nodes.src: Inscription base of obelisk, Hippodrome Constantinople (extant). Died 1 May 408.

nodes.label: Theodosius II
nodes.full: Longest-reigning emperor of the century; compiled the Theodosian Code, built the great walls.
nodes.src: Theodosian Code promulgated 15 Feb 438. Theodosian Walls 413 AD (still standing). Died horse accident 28 Jul 450.

nodes.label: Marcian
nodes.full: Military officer who married empress Pulcheria to legitimise his claim; called Chalcedon.
nodes.src: Council of Chalcedon 451 convened under him — acts survive. Ivory consular diptych 451 extant.

nodes.label: Leo I
nodes.full: First emperor formally crowned by the Patriarch of Constantinople.
nodes.src: Ceremony attested Theophanes Confessor. Novellae survive.

nodes.label: Zeno
nodes.full: Isaurian general; seized sole rule on son's death, twice exiled and restored.
nodes.src: Henotikon edict 482 — text in Evagrius Scholasticus HE III.14.

nodes.label: Battle of Pollentia
nodes.full: Stilicho checks Alaric's Visigoths in northern Italy; fought on Easter Sunday.
nodes.src: Claudian's poem De Bello Gothico composed 402 — primary near-contemporary source.

nodes.label: Rhine crossing
nodes.full: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the frozen Rhine, breaching the western frontier for good.
nodes.src: Jerome Letter 123 (written 409) describes devastation. Hydatius begins his chronicle from this event.

nodes.label: Sack of Rome by Alaric
nodes.full: Visigoths under Alaric sack Rome — first time the city falls to an enemy in 800 years.
nodes.src: Jerome Letters 127 & 128 (written 411) react directly. Augustine begins City of God partly in response.

nodes.label: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
nodes.full: Aetius and allied Visigoths halt Attila's invasion of Gaul; Visigoth king Theodoric I killed.
nodes.src: Jordanes Getica 197–218; Hydatius Chronicle §150. One of the largest battles of late antiquity.

nodes.label: Attila invades Italy
nodes.full: Attila destroys Aquileia; Pope Leo I meets him at the Mincio and he withdraws.
nodes.src: Hydatius §146; Prosper of Aquitaine records Leo's meeting. Attila dies 453.

nodes.label: Vandal Sack of Rome
nodes.full: Gaiseric's Vandals loot Rome for 14 days; Pope Leo I negotiates against burning.
nodes.src: Prosper of Aquitaine (primary contemporary) records 14-day sack.

nodes.label: Majorian's fleet destroyed
nodes.full: Vandals intercept and burn the Roman fleet at Cartagena before it can reach Africa.
nodes.src: John of Antioch fr.201.5 records it. Ends Majorian's reconquest plans.

nodes.label: Battle of Cape Bon
nodes.full: Combined East-West fleet of ~1,100 ships destroyed by Vandal fire ships.
nodes.src: Procopius BV I.6. Massive financial blow; effectively ends attempts to retake Africa.

nodes.label: Odoacer deposes Romulus
nodes.full: Germanic foederati revolt at Pavia; Odoacer exiles the last Western emperor.
nodes.src: Marcellinus Comes records date. Odoacer sends imperial regalia to Constantinople.

nodes.label: Odoacer vs. Zeno (diplomatic standoff)
nodes.full: Odoacer rules Italy while nominally acknowledging Eastern overlordship.
nodes.src: Cassiodorus Variae provide correspondence framework.

nodes.label: Theodosian Walls constructed
nodes.full: Massive double land-wall encircling Constantinople, still standing today.
nodes.src: Construction inscriptions survive in situ (Istanbul). Inner wall 5m thick, 12m high.

nodes.label: Theodosian Code promulgated
nodes.full: First systematic compilation of Roman imperial law — 16 books of edicts.
nodes.src: Senate readings recorded in acta — transcripts survive (Gesta Senatus). Codex Vossianus (Leiden) key MS.

nodes.label: Majorian: Novel I — military reform
nodes.full: Reforms conscription and addresses mass desertion in a crumbling Western army.
nodes.src: Survives in manuscript. One of seven surviving Majorian Novellae, each precisely dated.

nodes.label: Majorian: Novel VII — tax relief
nodes.full: Attempts to ease the crushing tax burden on the curial class.
nodes.src: Addresses tax burden on curiales. Explicitly dated. Survives in Novellarum Corpus.

nodes.label: Henotikon edict (Zeno)
nodes.full: Zeno's compromise formula trying to paper over the East's Christological split.
nodes.src: Full text in Evagrius Scholasticus HE III.14 (verbatim). Triggers Acacian Schism (484–519).

nodes.label: Acacian Schism declared
nodes.full: Pope Felix III excommunicates Patriarch Acacius; East and West formally split.
nodes.src: Letter of excommunication survives (Epistola XVI in papal register). Schism lasts 35 years.

nodes.label: Notitia Dignitatum compiled
nodes.full: Illustrated register of all military and civil offices of the entire Roman state.
nodes.src: Survives in medieval copies of a lost Carolingian original.

nodes.label: Council of Ephesus I
nodes.full: 200+ bishops condemn Nestorius's teaching that Mary was not 'Mother of God'.
nodes.src: Acts survive in Greek and Latin manuscripts. Nestorius deposed.

nodes.label: Council of Ephesus II ('Robber Synod')
nodes.full: Packed council reverses Ephesus I — Pope Leo calls it a 'robber synod'.
nodes.src: Pope Leo I's Tomus ad Flavianum (449) rejected here. Overturned at Chalcedon.

nodes.label: Council of Chalcedon
nodes.full: Defines Christ as fully divine and fully human — the foundational Christological formula.
nodes.src: 451 bishops. Acts survive in full (Concilium Chalcedonense, ACO II).

nodes.label: Pope Leo I: Tomus ad Flavianum
nodes.full: Leo's letter defining the 'two natures' of Christ, acclaimed at Chalcedon 451.
nodes.src: Survives in hundreds of manuscripts. Foundation of Chalcedonian Christology.

nodes.label: Jerome dies
nodes.full: Translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible; his death ends the last great Latin Church Father.
nodes.src: Vulgate (completed c.405) — earliest copy: Codex Amiatinus (c.692).

nodes.label: Patrick's mission to Ireland
nodes.full: Romano-British bishop establishes Christianity in Ireland; two texts in his own hand survive.
nodes.src: Confessio and Epistola ad Coroticum internally datable to mid-5th c. No external anchor confirmed.

nodes.label: Missorium of Theodosius I
nodes.full: 74cm silver dish commemorating Theodosius's tenth regnal year; depicts the imperial court.
nodes.src: Inscription confirms 388. Found 1847.

nodes.label: Diptych of Stilicho
nodes.full: Ivory consular diptych portrait of the Western generalissimo with his wife and son.
nodes.src: Key image of a non-imperial power-holder in late Roman court dress.

nodes.label: Mausoleum of Galla Placidia
nodes.full: Small cross-shaped mausoleum with the oldest and best-preserved mosaic programme in Ravenna.
nodes.src: Still standing. Mosaic programme intact.

nodes.label: Baptistery of the Orthodox
nodes.full: Octagonal baptistery with a vivid dome mosaic of Christ's baptism.
nodes.src: Inscription of Bishop Neon survives inside. Begun c.400, completed c.450.

nodes.label: Column of Arcadius base reliefs
nodes.full: Triumphal column recording Gothic campaigns; column lost 1715 but pre-modern drawings survive.
nodes.src: Freshfield Album drawings (1574), Trinity College Cambridge.

nodes.label: Projecta Casket (Esquiline Treasure)
nodes.full: Silver-gilt wedding casket with pagan and Christian imagery, from a wealthy Roman household.
nodes.src: BM 1866,0520.1. Inscription 'SECUNDE ET PROJECTA VIVATIS IN CHRISTO'.

nodes.label: Sarcophagus of Stilicho
nodes.full: Marble sarcophagus likely from Stilicho's family; shows Christian funerary art for the elite.
nodes.src: Shows biblical scenes — example of Christian aristocratic funerary art.

nodes.label: Boethius: De Institutione Musica — music theory for the Middle Ages
nodes.full: Boethius writes the foundational text of Western music theory — synthesising Greek theory (Pythagoras, Ptolemy) for a Latin audience; it becomes the standard university music textbook for 1,000 years and shapes how European music is conceptualised.
nodes.src: De Institutione Musica: complete text survives. Earliest MS: 9th century. Bower translation (1989). Boethius distinguishes musica mundana (cosmic), musica humana (human harmony) and musica instrumentalis (performed music) — the tripartite framework inherited by all medieval music theory. Written c.500–510, just after Boethius served as consul (510). The text's influence: cited in every major medieval music treatise.

nodes.label: Augustine: City of God
nodes.full: 22-book rebuttal of pagans who blamed Christianity for Rome's fall.
nodes.src: Begun after 410 Sack. Oldest manuscript: uncial fragments 5th–6th c.

nodes.label: Orosius: Seven Books Against the Pagans
nodes.full: First universal history from a Christian perspective, written at Augustine's request.
nodes.src: Explicit date: book 7 written 'in the 1,164th year of the city' = 417 AD.

nodes.label: Hydatius: Chronicle
nodes.full: Bishop in NW Spain; eyewitness to Vandal raids — our main source for 5th-century Iberia.
nodes.src: Single 9th-c. copy survives (Madrid, Real Academia de la Historia).

nodes.label: Prosper of Aquitaine: Chronicle
nodes.full: Court insider who updates Jerome's chronicle; contemporary for Italian events from 425.
nodes.src: Survives in many MSS. Key for Italian events.

nodes.label: Priscus: History (fragments)
nodes.full: Diplomat who visited Attila's court in 449; his firsthand description is irreplaceable.
nodes.src: Survives in fragments (Exc. de Legationibus). Describes Attila's wooden palace and feasts.

nodes.label: Sidonius Apollinaris: Letters & Poems
nodes.full: Bishop of Clermont; 9 books of letters are an eyewitness record of Gaul's fall to Visigoths.
nodes.src: MSS from 9th c. onward. Carmen II (panegyric to Anthemius, 468) datable within days.

nodes.label: Olympiodorus of Thebes: History (fragments)
nodes.full: Egyptian diplomat who visited the Huns c.412; fragments cover the turbulent 407–425 period.
nodes.src: Fragments in Photius Bibliotheca (cod. 80).

nodes.label: Contraction of Western tax base
nodes.full: Loss of Africa, Spain and Gaul to barbarian kingdoms strips the Western court of most tax revenue.
nodes.src: Documented through Majorian's Novellae (458). Jones, LRE (1964) synthesises papyrus and law evidence.

nodes.label: Vandal seizure of North Africa
nodes.full: Vandals cross from Spain, take Carthage 439 — stripping Rome of its richest grain-producing province.
nodes.src: Prosper of Aquitaine records fall of Carthage 439. Coins of Gaiseric minted Carthage from 439.

nodes.label: Collapse of Western coinage
nodes.full: Western gold solidus production becomes erratic after 455; silver and bronze collapse almost entirely by 470s.
nodes.src: Numismatic evidence: die studies show sharp drop in Western mint output post-455. Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985).

nodes.label: Theodosian Walls engineering
nodes.full: The most sophisticated urban fortification of late antiquity — triple walls, 96 towers, a moat.
nodes.src: Construction inscriptions survive in situ. Outer wall added after 447 earthquake. Engineering described in Chronicon Paschale.

nodes.label: Roman road network in use
nodes.full: The road network — over 80,000 km — continued operating, documented in the Tabula Peutingeriana.
nodes.src: Tabula Peutingeriana: medieval copy (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Vienna, Cod. 324) of a late-Roman itinerary map.

nodes.label: Ravenna harbour and fleet base
nodes.full: Honorius's decision to base the Western court at Ravenna made its harbour the main Western naval base.
nodes.src: Archaeological evidence: Classis excavations. Sidonius Apollinaris Letter I.5 describes port activity c.461.

nodes.label: Codex replaces scroll (transition)
nodes.full: By 400 the codex (bound book) has almost entirely replaced the papyrus roll for Christian and legal texts.
nodes.src: Statistical evidence from papyrus finds: Roberts & Skeat, The Birth of the Codex (1983).

nodes.label: Priscus's embassy to Attila — firsthand diplomatic record
nodes.full: The Byzantine diplomat Priscus travels to Attila's court as part of an embassy — his account is the only firsthand description of Hunnic court culture, the physical appearance of Attila's settlement, and the mechanics of Roman-Hunnic diplomacy.
nodes.src: Priscus fragments: Exc. de Legationibus (Constantine VII's compilation). The embassy of 449 is datable. Priscus describes meeting a Greek merchant who had settled with the Huns voluntarily — one of the most striking cross-cultural encounters in the sources. MOVED from Thought tx5 — belongs here as a diplomatic record as much as an intellectual one.

nodes.label: Odoacer sends imperial regalia to Constantinople
nodes.full: After deposing Romulus Augustulus, Odoacer sends the Western imperial regalia to Constantinople with a message that one emperor is sufficient — a diplomatic act that simultaneously ends the Western Empire and asserts continuity with the East.
nodes.src: Marcellinus Comes records the regalia transfer. Malchus fragments (diplomat and historian, contemporary) on the subsequent negotiations. The diplomatic formula — Odoacer rules Italy in the name of Zeno — is documented in Cassiodorus. This is the key exchange that legally defines what 476 meant.

nodes.label: Vandal North Africa — disruption of Western Mediterranean trade
nodes.full: Vandal naval control of the Western Mediterranean from Carthage disrupts the grain and luxury trade routes that had sustained Rome for 500 years — the archaeological evidence (sharp decline in African Red Slip pottery in Western sites) is one of the clearest material signatures of the 5th-century economic collapse.
nodes.src: African Red Slip (ARS) pottery distribution: Hayes (1972), Late Roman Pottery — the standard reference. Dramatic decline in ARS at Western sites post-439 documented in multiple excavation reports. Wickham (2005), Framing the Early Middle Ages, ch.2: synthesises the evidence for trade collapse. This is the best-evidenced material trace of the Western Empire's economic unravelling.

nodes.label: Sidonius Apollinaris — Roman aristocratic culture persisting in Visigothic Gaul
nodes.full: Sidonius Apollinaris's letters document the extraordinary cultural negotiation between Roman aristocratic literary culture and the new Visigothic kingdom — he praises Gothic kings in Latin verse, teaches Roman rhetoric to Gallo-Roman nobles under Gothic rule, and records the terms of cultural survival.
nodes.src: Sidonius Apollinaris, Epistulae (9 books, extant). Letters to King Euric: Ep. 7.6. Description of Theoderic II's court: Ep. 1.2 — a unique ethnographic account. Harries (1994), Sidonius Apollinaris and the Fall of Rome. This is the richest single source for cultural transmission across the Roman-barbarian boundary.

nodes.label: Hunnic displacement cascade
nodes.full: Hunnic westward expansion pushes entire Gothic peoples across Roman frontiers, triggering a chain reaction.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus res gestae 31 records Goths crossing Danube 376. Physical evidence: Hunnic cauldrons found across Pontic steppe.

nodes.label: Earthquake, Constantinople
nodes.full: Major quake collapses sections of the Theodosian Walls — repaired in 60 days with Attila's army approaching.
nodes.src: Surviving inscription on restored tower records Prefect Cyrus rebuilt 57 towers in 60 days.

nodes.label: Plague: Spain and Gaul
nodes.full: Epidemic outbreaks noted in two independent contemporary sources; pathogen unknown.
nodes.src: Hydatius Chronicle §129 records 446 in Spain. Sidonius letter V.14 mentions c.467 in Gaul.

nodes.label: Attila's death and Hunnic collapse
nodes.full: Attila dies the night of his wedding; the Hunnic empire immediately disintegrates.
nodes.src: Jordanes Getica 254; Priscus fragment 24. Hunnic sons fight Battle of Nedao (454).

nodes.label: Late Roman climatic shift (LALIA precursor)
nodes.full: Tree-ring and ice-core data suggest climatic instability beginning mid-5th c., possibly contributing to agricultural stress.
nodes.src: Evidence: Büntgen et al. (2016), Science 352 — Alpine tree-ring records. LALIA onset c.536 but precursor instability visible from c.450.

nodes.label: Galla Placidia — regent empress and political actor
nodes.full: Galla Placidia rules as regent for her son Valentinian III for 14 years — issuing laws, commanding armies through generals, and commissioning the Ravenna mosaics; her political authority is extensively documented in imperial legislation and court records.
nodes.src: Imperial laws issued under her regency: Codex Theodosianus and later Novels. Oost (1968), Galla Placidia Augusta: the standard biography. Her Ravenna mausoleum (extant, UNESCO) as a monument to self-representation. Coins: she appears on solidi as Augusta — numismatic evidence of official status. McEvoy (2013), Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West.

nodes.label: Female saints passing as monks — the transvestite saints
nodes.full: A genre of hagiography emerges: women living as male monks (Pelagia, Marinos/Mary, Eugenia) — these texts are not straightforward transgender evidence but document a cultural category of gender crossing that the Church simultaneously recorded and sanctified.
nodes.src: Vita Pelagiae (Syriac and Greek, 5th c.): AASS October 8. Vita Marini (Latin, 5th c.): collected in PL 73. Anson (1974), The Female Transvestite in Early Monasticism, Viator 5. Davis (2002), Crossed Texts, Crossed Sex: Intertextuality and Gender in Early Christian Legends of Holy Women Disguised as Men. These texts are primarily prescriptive/literary but document the cultural legibility of gender crossing.

nodes.label: Codex Theodosianus on enslaved persons — legal personhood denied
nodes.full: The Theodosian Code systematically codifies enslaved persons' legal non-personhood alongside the laws of the Christian empire — the co-existence of Christian theology (all souls equal before God) and legal chattel slavery is here most starkly documented.
nodes.src: CTh Book 2 (on contracts) and Book 9 (on criminal law): multiple provisions treating enslaved persons as property. Harper (2011), Slavery in the Late Roman World. The theological contradiction: Augustine's nuanced position on slavery in City of God 19.15 vs. the legal code. This tension is itself a historical fact about the period.
